checks.text: Each of its places holds a faint fixed source: 6 other D4 exposures of other days measure 364 ± 34 µJy (10.8σ) there, 0.79× the circled dot: a star just under the cut can make such a dot without anything moving.
checks.look: In the Viewer's hours clock on D4, open other days of the visit at this place: something faint stays at the circle.

checks.text: CatWISE2020 lists a W1 16.4, W2 16.0 source 2.3″ south-east of its middle position: it may be that source (a faint star seen in only some exposures, or a dot on its edge) rather than something that moves. By chance alone, 8% of spots here have a CatWISE2020 source this close (44% within 6″).
checks.look: On the hours clock in D4, blink its exposures: if every dot sits on the catalogued spot (2.3″ south-east of the middle) it is that source; a mover's dots step across it.

checks.text: D1 shows 647 ± 111 µJy at its place at the same moment, but about as much (1,018 ± 97 µJy) at that spot on other days: that is a fixed source there, so the colour test can't tell whether D1 saw it.
checks.look: In the Viewer's hours clock, switch to D1 at 30 May 2025, 19:18 UTC: something sits at the circle in every photo.

checks.text: Light from something next to it spills into its places on other days: 6 other D4 exposures measure 563 ± 30 µJy there, centred 5.5″ away (0.70× the circled dot): check that the dot isn't part of that neighbour.
checks.look: In the Viewer's hours clock on D4, compare the circle with other days of the visit: a source sits just beside it.

candidates.why: Seen at different places in 3 exposures over 4.3 minutes, moving about 82″ an hour; the nearest known asteroid, comet, planet or moon was predicted 7.8′ away.

checks.text: D1 photographed the same spot at the same moment and measured 195 ± 66 µJy against 485 µJy in D4: D4/D1 ≥ 1.24 (3σ), redder than every known asteroid we measured (known 0.24–1.1). Seen in D4 alone, which real asteroids almost never are (1 in 200) but D4 glitches often are.
checks.look: In the Viewer's hours clock, switch between D4 and D1 at 31 May 2025, 01:47 UTC: the dot is in D4 only.

checks.text: Each of its places holds a fixed source: 5 other D4 exposures of other days measure 508 ± 35 µJy (14.7σ) there, 0.98× the circled dot: that source is bright enough to be seen in each photo, so the dot is most likely it, not something moving.
checks.look: In the Viewer's hours clock on D4, open other days of the visit at this place: something faint stays at the circle.

checks.text: CatWISE2020 lists a W1 15.9, W2 15.5 source 4.5″ north-west of its middle position: it may be that source (a faint star seen in only some exposures, or a dot on its edge) rather than something that moves. By chance alone, 22% of spots here have a CatWISE2020 source this close (35% within 6″).
checks.look: On the hours clock in D4, blink its exposures: if every dot sits on the catalogued spot (4.5″ north-west of the middle) it is that source; a mover's dots step across it.

checks.text: The known asteroid 2011 QT9 (MPC orbit, V 23.0) was predicted 38″ to the west of it, moving 85″ an hour toward PA 79°; ours moves 82″ an hour toward PA 309°. Not a certain match: it is 49″ off at the farthest dot, the directions differ by 131°.
checks.look: On the hours clock in D4, step through its exposures and look 38″ to the west: if a second moving dot runs there, that is 2011 QT9 and ours is something else; if not, ours may be 2011 QT9 slightly off its predicted place.

checks.text: 2 of its 3 dots are 1.45–1.46× as wide as the stars of the same brightness in the same photos, while known asteroids' dots measure 0.8–1.3×: a smudge, not a sharp moving point (noise or two faint things blended, unless it is a comet's haze).
checks.look: In the Viewer's hours clock on D4, exposure of 31 May 2025, 01:47 UTC: compare the dot with stars of similar brightness around it; it is softer and broader.
